glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: The LORD sends Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh with His purpose declared, “the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD,” and opens the confrontation as Aaron’s rod swallows the magicians’ rods and the waters of Egypt are turned to blood.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Exodus 7 answers Moses’ protest in 6:30 and completes his commission. With verse 8 the plagues on Egypt begin, the third major movement of the book.

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:
• Exodus 7:1–7 — The LORD Sends Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh

  • Exodus 7:8–13 — Aaron’s Rod Swallows the Magicians’ Rods

  • Exodus 7:14–25 — The LORD Turns the Waters of Egypt to Blood

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “And the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out My hand on Egypt and bring out the children of Israel from among them.’” (Exodus 7:5)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
God settles Moses’ objections by assigning roles. Moses will be “as God to Pharaoh” (7:1), bringing God’s word with God’s authority, and Aaron will speak for him. The LORD also announces the shape of what is coming: He will harden Pharaoh’s heart and multiply His signs, and through great judgments “the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD” (7:5). Pharaoh had asked, “Who is the LORD?” (5:2). The answer now begins.

The first sign is given in Pharaoh’s court. Aaron’s rod becomes a serpent, and Egypt’s magicians do the same, “But Aaron’s rod swallowed up their rods” (7:12). Then the LORD strikes the Nile, the source of Egypt’s water, food, and life. The river turns to blood, the fish die, and the people dig for water. The magicians manage a small imitation, which only gives Pharaoh an excuse. He goes into his house, and “Neither was his heart moved by this” (7:23). Each time the narrator adds, “as the LORD had said.” Pharaoh resists freely, and yet nothing he does falls outside what God foretold.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Exodus 7:1–7 — The LORD Sends Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh

The LORD makes Moses “as God to Pharaoh” with Aaron as his prophet, and He announces that He will harden Pharaoh’s heart and multiply His signs so that Egypt will know He is the LORD. Moses, eighty, and Aaron, eighty-three, obey.

Exodus 7:8–13 — Aaron’s Rod Swallows the Magicians’ Rods

Before Pharaoh, Aaron’s rod becomes a serpent, and the magicians copy the sign with their enchantments. Aaron’s rod swallows theirs, yet Pharaoh’s heart grows hard, as the LORD had said.

Exodus 7:14–25 — The LORD Turns the Waters of Egypt to Blood

At the river the LORD declares, “By this you shall know that I am the LORD” (7:17), and the waters of Egypt turn to blood, killing the fish and leaving the people without water. The magicians imitate the sign, Pharaoh walks away unmoved, and the Egyptians dig around the river for water to drink. Seven days pass after the LORD strikes the river.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Exodus 7 shows that the plagues are revelation as well as judgment. God says why He acts: so that Egypt will know who He is. The Nile was Egypt’s lifeline and was honored in its religion, and the LORD struck it first. Later He declares judgment “against all the gods of Egypt” (12:12).

The chapter also shows how God’s sovereignty and Pharaoh’s responsibility stand together. God announces the hardening beforehand, and Pharaoh still chooses to turn away and refuses to take the judgment to heart. Counterfeit power could imitate a little but could not undo anything God had done.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Knowing the LORD. God acts so that Egypt will know that He is the LORD (7:5, 17).

Pharaoh’s hard heart. God announces the hardening, and Pharaoh refuses to heed or take the sign to heart (7:3, 13, 22–23).

The LORD over Egypt’s power. Aaron’s rod swallows the magicians’ rods, and the life-giving river is struck (7:12, 20–21).

Obedience to God’s word. Moses and Aaron do “just as the LORD commanded” (7:10, 20), and events unfold “as the LORD had said” (7:13, 22).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
As God to Pharaoh (7:1). Moses’ assigned role as God’s commissioned servant: he brings God’s words and works to Pharaoh, and Aaron speaks for him.

Prophet (7:1). One who speaks for another. Aaron speaks Moses’ message, just as a prophet speaks God’s message.

Magicians (7:11). Pharaoh’s wise men and sorcerers. Their limited imitation, whether trickery or counterfeit spiritual power, only hardened Pharaoh and could not reverse the judgment.

The river (7:15–25). The Nile, the source of Egypt’s water, food, and life, which God strikes in the first plague.

focus: Exodus 7 completes the LORD’s renewed commission to Moses and Aaron and then opens the confrontation with Pharaoh through signs and judgments. The chapter moves from God’s announced purpose that the Egyptians shall know that He is the LORD, to Aaron’s rod swallowing the magicians’ rods, to the waters of Egypt turned to blood while Pharaoh’s heart remains hard.

sections.title: The LORD Sends Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh
sections.summary: The LORD makes Moses “as God to Pharaoh” with Aaron as his prophet, and He announces that He will harden Pharaoh’s heart and multiply His signs so that “the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD” (Exodus 7:5). Moses and Aaron do as the LORD commands, at eighty and eighty-three years old.

sections.title: Aaron’s Rod Swallows the Magicians’ Rods
sections.summary: Aaron casts down his rod before Pharaoh and it becomes a serpent, and Egypt’s magicians do the same with their enchantments. “Aaron’s rod swallowed up their rods” (Exodus 7:12), yet Pharaoh’s heart grows hard, as the LORD had said.

sections.title: The LORD Turns the Waters of Egypt to Blood
sections.summary: At the river the LORD tells Pharaoh, “By this you shall know that I am the LORD” (Exodus 7:17), and the waters of Egypt are turned to blood, so that the fish die and the people cannot drink. When the magicians imitate the sign, Pharaoh’s heart grows hard, and he does not heed them or take the judgment to heart; the Egyptians dig around the river for water to drink, and seven days pass after the LORD strikes the river.

1.brief: The LORD tells Moses, “See, I have made you as God to Pharaoh,” with Aaron as his prophet. Moses will stand before Pharaoh with God’s authority, and Aaron will speak for him.
1.explain:
“So the LORD said to Moses: ‘See, I have made you as God to Pharaoh,”

God answers Moses’ objection about his speech (6:30). Moses will stand before Pharaoh with God’s authority. To Pharaoh, Moses will be “as God,” the one who speaks God’s word and through whom God’s power comes. The comparison describes Moses’ role, not his nature. He remains God’s commissioned servant. Pharaoh claimed divine status in Egypt, but he will face a shepherd carrying the authority of the true God.

“and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet.”

Aaron will be Moses’ “prophet.” A prophet speaks for someone else. As a prophet speaks God’s words, Aaron will speak Moses’ words. This echoes 4:16.
1.notes: The Hebrew word translated “prophet” refers to a spokesman who speaks on behalf of another. This verse gives one of the clearest pictures in Scripture of what a prophet is.

2.brief: Moses is to speak all that God commands, and Aaron is to tell Pharaoh to send Israel out of his land. The message passes from God to Moses to Aaron to Pharaoh.
2.explain:
“You shall speak all that I command you.”

Moses’ job is to speak “all” God commands. He is not free to change the message.

“And Aaron your brother shall tell Pharaoh to send the children of Israel out of his land.”

Aaron will deliver the message to Pharaoh. The message passes from God to Moses to Aaron to Pharaoh.

3.brief: God declares, “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart,” and multiply His signs and wonders in Egypt. God announces in advance that Pharaoh’s resistance will become the occasion for many more signs.
3.explain:
“And I will harden Pharaoh’s heart,”

God declares in advance that He will “harden Pharaoh’s heart.” This was announced first in 4:21. Pharaoh has already shown that he will not acknowledge the LORD (5:2). God will confirm Pharaoh in the stubbornness he has chosen. Pharaoh remains responsible for his refusal, and God carries out His purpose through it.

“and multiply My signs and My wonders in the land of Egypt.”

Pharaoh’s resistance will become the occasion for many more “signs” and “wonders.” Each refusal will bring another display of God’s power. God announces in advance that Pharaoh’s resistance will lead to many more signs.
3.notes: The Hebrew verb translated “harden” in this verse means to make hard or stubborn. A different verb is used in 4:21. Exodus uses several verbs for hardening, and their exact differences should not be pressed.

4.brief: Pharaoh will not heed them, so that God may lay His hand on Egypt and bring out “My armies and My people” by great judgments. Pharaoh’s refusal will lead to God’s judgments and Israel’s release.
4.explain:
“But Pharaoh will not heed you,”

God tells Moses ahead of time that Pharaoh “will not heed” him. Moses should not be discouraged when Pharaoh refuses. God has already said it will happen.

“so that I may lay My hand on Egypt and bring My armies and My people, the children of Israel, out of the land of Egypt by great judgments.”

Pharaoh’s refusal will lead to God laying His “hand on Egypt.” God calls Israel “My armies and My people.” The slaves are His host. He will bring them out “by great judgments” on Egypt. Pharaoh’s refusal will lead to God’s judgments and Israel’s release.

5.brief: “And the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD” when God stretches out His hand and brings Israel out. God’s purpose reaches beyond Israel to make Himself known to Egypt.
5.explain:
“And the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD,”

God’s purpose reaches beyond Israel. Pharaoh asked, “Who is the LORD?” (5:2). Egypt will learn the answer. God makes Himself known even to those who oppose Him.

“when I stretch out My hand on Egypt and bring out the children of Israel from among them.”

The Egyptians will come to know the LORD through His power displayed in judgment and in Israel’s deliverance. God’s purpose reaches beyond Israel to make Himself known to Egypt.
5.notes: The phrase “know that I am the LORD” is a recurring theme in Exodus. It is used of Israel (6:7; 10:2; 16:12), of Pharaoh (7:17; 8:22), and of the Egyptians (7:5; 14:4, 18).

6.brief: Moses and Aaron do just as the LORD commands them. After Moses’ repeated objections, the brothers now obey together.
6.explain:
“Then Moses and Aaron did so; just as the LORD commanded them, so they did.”

After Moses’ repeated objections, the brothers now obey together. The verse states their obedience twice: they “did so,” and “so they did.” From this point on, Moses raises no further objection to his commission.

7.brief: Moses is eighty years old and Aaron eighty-three when they speak to Pharaoh. The note marks the start of their confrontation with Pharaoh and closes the account of their commission.
7.explain:
“And Moses was eighty years old and Aaron eighty-three years old when they spoke to Pharaoh.”

Moses was “eighty years old,” and Aaron “eighty-three.” These were not young men. God called them at an age when many people expect their work to be done. Moses spent forty years in Egypt and forty years in Midian before this moment (Acts 7:23, 30). The note marks the start of their confrontation with Pharaoh and closes the account of their commission.
7.notes: Moses would live to be 120 years old (Deuteronomy 34:7), giving his life three periods of about forty years each: Egypt, Midian, and the wilderness.

8.brief: The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron. A new stage begins as God prepares them for their first sign before Pharaoh.
8.explain:
“Then the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying,”

God speaks to both brothers. A new stage begins as God prepares them for their first sign before Pharaoh.

9.brief: When Pharaoh demands a miracle, Aaron is to cast his rod before Pharaoh, and it will become a serpent. God anticipates Pharaoh’s challenge and provides the sign.
9.explain:
“When Pharaoh speaks to you, saying, ‘Show a miracle for yourselves,”

God anticipates that Pharaoh will demand proof. Pharaoh will want evidence that these men speak for a real god.

“then you shall say to Aaron, ‘Take your rod and cast it before Pharaoh, and let it become a serpent.”

The sign will be the rod becoming a “serpent.” God anticipates Pharaoh’s challenge and provides the sign.
9.notes: The Hebrew word translated “serpent” here differs from the word in 4:3. This word can refer to a large reptile, such as a snake or crocodile, or a sea creature (Genesis 1:21, “great sea creatures”).

10.brief: Moses and Aaron go to Pharaoh and do as the LORD commanded, and Aaron’s rod becomes a serpent before Pharaoh and his servants. The first sign is given in the king’s own presence.
10.explain:
“So Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh, and they did so, just as the LORD commanded.”

The brothers obey exactly. They do “just as the LORD commanded.”

“And Aaron cast down his rod before Pharaoh and before his servants, and it became a serpent.”

Aaron throws down the rod, and it becomes a serpent. The first sign is given in the king’s own presence, before his officials.

11.brief: Pharaoh calls his wise men and sorcerers, and Egypt’s magicians do the same with their enchantments.
11.explain:
“But Pharaoh also called the wise men and the sorcerers;”

Pharaoh calls his own experts: “the wise men and the sorcerers.” These were the learned men of Egypt’s court, skilled in secret arts.

“so the magicians of Egypt, they also did in like manner with their enchantments.”

The “magicians” did the same thing “with their enchantments,” secret arts or occult practices. The text does not explain how they did it, whether by trickery or by demonic power. Egypt’s magicians imitated the sign through their enchantments.
11.notes:
Paul names two of these magicians, Jannes and Jambres, as men who “resisted Moses” (2 Timothy 3:8). Their names come from Jewish tradition and do not appear in Exodus.

The Hebrew word translated “enchantments” refers to secret arts. A similar word is used in 7:22 and 8:7.

12.brief: Each magician throws down his rod and it becomes a serpent, “But Aaron’s rod swallowed up their rods.” The sign shows the LORD’s power overcoming everything Egypt can match.
12.explain:
“For every man threw down his rod, and they became serpents.”

Each magician throws down his rod, and each becomes a serpent. For a moment it looks as though Egypt’s power matches God’s.

“But Aaron’s rod swallowed up their rods.”

Then the tables turned. God’s power overcomes everything Egypt can match. The magicians could imitate, but they could not prevail. The sign shows the LORD’s power overcoming Egypt’s.

13.brief: Pharaoh’s heart grows hard, and he does not heed them, “as the LORD had said.” Pharaoh’s refusal unfolds exactly as God foretold.
13.explain:
“And Pharaoh’s heart grew hard, and he did not heed them, as the LORD had said.”

Despite what he has seen, Pharaoh’s heart “grew hard.” He refuses to listen. The phrase “as the LORD had said” shows that nothing is out of God’s control. Pharaoh’s refusal unfolds exactly as God foretold (7:3–4).
13.notes: The Hebrew verb translated “grew hard” in this verse means to become strong or firm. The NKJV wording describes Pharaoh’s heart as becoming hard without naming who hardened it.

14.brief: The LORD tells Moses, “Pharaoh’s heart is hard; he refuses to let the people go.” God names Pharaoh’s settled resistance as the reason for the coming judgment.
14.explain:
“So the LORD said to Moses: ‘Pharaoh’s heart is hard; he refuses to let the people go.”

God diagnoses Pharaoh’s condition. His heart “is hard.” He “refuses” to let Israel go. God names Pharaoh’s settled resistance as the reason for the coming judgment.
14.notes: The Hebrew word translated “hard” here means heavy. The same root is used for glory, the weight of God’s presence. Pharaoh’s heart is heavy, unmoved and dull toward God.

15.brief: Moses is to meet Pharaoh in the morning by the river’s bank, taking the rod that became a serpent. The first plague will begin at the river, the center of Egypt’s life.
15.explain:
“Go to Pharaoh in the morning, when he goes out to the water,”

Moses is to meet Pharaoh “in the morning, when he goes out to the water.” The text does not say why Pharaoh went to the Nile each morning. He may have gone to bathe, to inspect the water level, or for religious reasons.

“and you shall stand by the river’s bank to meet him;”

Moses will confront Pharaoh at “the river’s bank.” The Nile was the source of Egypt’s life, its water, food, and wealth. The first plague will begin at the river, the center of Egypt’s life.

“and the rod which was turned to a serpent you shall take in your hand.”

Moses must carry the rod. Pharaoh would recognize it as the rod that swallowed his magicians’ rods.

16.brief: Moses is to tell Pharaoh that the LORD God of the Hebrews sent him to say, “Let My people go, that they may serve Me in the wilderness,” though Pharaoh has not listened. The LORD’s demand is repeated before judgment falls.
16.explain:
“And you shall say to him, ‘The LORD God of the Hebrews has sent me to you, saying,”

Moses must speak in the name of “the LORD God of the Hebrews.” He comes as God’s messenger.

“Let My people go, that they may serve Me in the wilderness’;”

The demand is the same. God’s people must be released to “serve” Him. The word recalls the forced service Israel gave Pharaoh (1:13–14). They must be free to serve the LORD.

“but indeed, until now you would not hear!”

God notes that Pharaoh has refused to listen “until now.” The LORD’s demand is repeated before judgment falls.

17.brief: The LORD declares, “By this you shall know that I am the LORD,” and warns that the river will be struck and turned to blood. The plague is a sign that will reveal who the LORD is.
17.explain:
“Thus says the LORD: ‘By this you shall know that I am the LORD.”

The purpose of the plague is stated first. “By this you shall know that I am the LORD.” Pharaoh said, “I do not know the LORD” (5:2). This plague is God’s answer.

“Behold, I will strike the waters which are in the river with the rod that is in my hand, and they shall be turned to blood.”

The “waters” of the Nile “shall be turned to blood.” The source of Egypt’s life will become a sign of death. The river where Hebrew boys had been thrown to die (1:22) becomes blood. The plague is a sign that will reveal who the LORD is.
17.notes:
The speaker shifts within the verse. God speaks, but “the rod that is in my hand” refers to Moses’ rod. Moses speaks God’s word, and God acts through Moses’ hand.

Interpreters have suggested that some plagues confronted specific Egyptian gods, such as gods associated with the Nile. Exodus 12:12 says God would execute judgment on “all the gods of Egypt,” but the text does not link each plague to a particular god.

18.brief: The fish in the river will die, the river will stink, and the Egyptians will loathe to drink its water. The judgment will strike the source of Egypt’s water and food.
18.explain:
“And the fish that are in the river shall die, the river shall stink,”

The plague will kill the fish and make the river “stink.” Fish were a major part of Egypt’s food supply.

“and the Egyptians will loathe to drink the water of the river.”

The Egyptians will “loathe” to drink it. They will be repulsed. The judgment will strike the source of Egypt’s water and food.

19.brief: The LORD tells Moses to have Aaron take his rod and stretch out his hand over Egypt’s streams, rivers, ponds, and pools, so that they become blood throughout the land, even in vessels of wood and stone. The plague will reach the waters of Egypt far beyond the river itself.
19.explain:
“Then the LORD spoke to Moses, ‘Say to Aaron, ‘Take your rod and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt,”

God tells Moses to have Aaron stretch out the rod “over the waters of Egypt.”

“over their streams, over their rivers, over their ponds, and over all their pools of water, that they may become blood.”

The plague will reach every kind of water: “streams,” the branches of the Nile in the delta, “rivers,” likely the irrigation canals, “ponds,” and “pools.” All of Egypt’s water will turn to blood.

“And there shall be blood throughout all the land of Egypt, both in buckets of wood and pitchers of stone.”

Even water already stored “in buckets of wood and pitchers of stone” will turn to blood. The plague will reach the waters of Egypt far beyond the river itself.
19.notes: The Hebrew word translated “streams” here refers to the branches of the Nile. The word translated “rivers” likely refers to canals.

20.brief: Moses and Aaron do as the LORD commanded, and when the rod strikes the river before Pharaoh and his servants, all the water in the river turns to blood. God’s word is carried out in public view.
20.explain:
“And Moses and Aaron did so, just as the LORD commanded.”

The brothers obey exactly.

“So he lifted up the rod and struck the waters that were in the river, in the sight of Pharaoh and in the sight of his servants.”

The rod strikes the river “in the sight of Pharaoh and in the sight of his servants.” No one could claim it happened in secret.

“And all the waters that were in the river were turned to blood.”

“All the waters” turned to blood. God’s word is carried out in public view.

21.brief: The fish die, the river stinks, the Egyptians cannot drink its water, and there is blood throughout Egypt. Everything God announced in verse 18 comes to pass.
21.explain:
“The fish that were in the river died, the river stank, and the Egyptians could not drink the water of the river.”

Everything God said would happen happened. The “fish” died, the river “stank,” and the Egyptians could not drink.

“So there was blood throughout all the land of Egypt.”

The plague spread “throughout all the land of Egypt.” Everything God announced in 7:18 came to pass.

22.brief: The magicians do the same with their enchantments, and Pharaoh’s heart grows hard, and he does not heed them, “as the LORD had said.” Pharaoh’s hardened heart and refusal to listen come just as the LORD foretold, even as the magicians imitate the sign.
22.explain:
“Then the magicians of Egypt did so with their enchantments;”

The magicians imitated the sign. They made water turn to blood. Their imitation did nothing to help Egypt. It only added to the problem. The narrative records their imitation and that the plague continued. It does not say whether they tried to reverse it.

“and Pharaoh’s heart grew hard, and he did not heed them, as the LORD had said.”

Pharaoh’s heart “grew hard.” He refused to listen. Pharaoh’s hardened heart and refusal to listen came just as the LORD foretold, even as the magicians imitated the sign.
22.notes: Where the magicians found water to turn into blood is not explained. The water dug from wells around the river (7:24) is one possibility.

23.brief: Pharaoh turns and goes into his house, “Neither was his heart moved by this.” He walks away from the judgment without taking it to heart.
23.explain:
“And Pharaoh turned and went into his house.”

Pharaoh simply “turned and went into his house.” He walked away.

“Neither was his heart moved by this.”

Pharaoh did not take it to heart. The phrase means he did not let it affect him or consider what it meant. He walked away from the judgment without taking it to heart.

24.brief: All the Egyptians dig around the river for water to drink, because they cannot drink from the river. The people of Egypt suffer the consequences of their king’s refusal.
24.explain:
“So all the Egyptians dug all around the river for water to drink,”

The Egyptians “dug all around the river” looking for water. They dug wells near the river, hoping to find water that had filtered through the ground.

“because they could not drink the water of the river.”

They could not drink from the Nile. The people of Egypt suffered the consequences of their king’s refusal.

25.brief: Seven days pass after the LORD struck the river. The note marks the time before the next plague and names the LORD as the One who struck the river.
25.explain:
“And seven days passed after the LORD had struck the river.”

The plague lasted “seven days.” The verse names “the LORD” as the One who “struck the river.” Aaron held the rod, but God brought the plague. The note marks the time before the next plague.
